question_text: USB uses a D+ and D- data line. What is this routing technique called, and what is its primary advantage for noise immunity?
answer_text: It is called Differential Signaling. Its primary advantage is that it completely rejects "common-mode" noise.
explanation_text: Instead of sending a single voltage relative to ground, the transmitter sends mirrored signals: when D+ goes high, D- goes equally low. The receiver only looks at the *difference* between the two wires. If external electromagnetic noise (EMI) strikes the cable, it couples equally into both wires (adding the exact same noise voltage to both). Because the receiver subtracts D- from D+, the noise perfectly cancels itself out!
bonus_question_text: Why is it critical that D+ and D- traces are routed to be the exact same physical length on a PCB?
bonus_answer_text: To prevent "skew." If one trace is longer, its signal arrives a fraction of a nanosecond later. This misalignment destroys the common-mode noise rejection and severely degrades the signal's eye diagram.
